title: EMA Crossback
teaches: The EMA Crossback as we trade it: the first pullback into the rising short averages after a stock has turned up out of a decline (a Wedge Pop) or broken out, a hold day that reaches the zone and closes at or above the 20 EMA in the upper half of its range, the buy is the trade a few cents over the hold day's high within three sessions, the stop sits a few cents under the hold day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the system working.

walkthroughs.title: UAA, June 2015: the clean stair-step
steps: UAA in June 2015, a leader in a clean stair-step. It pops on 1.5 times volume, then drifts back two quiet sessions.
The hold day dips into the 9 and 20 EMA zone and closes over the 20. The 9 stays above it.
June 16 it trades over the hold day's high. Buy at market, 40.82. Stop just under the hold day's low, 40.17.
Lose the hold day's low and you're out. It held. 3R in 5 days, and that push is where I'd sell some.

walkthroughs.title: CLS, October 2024: the undercut that held
steps: CLS pops on 1.1 times volume in September 2024, then drifts down to its averages for four quiet days.
The hold day undercuts the 20 EMA by 0.6% and closes back over it. That's still inside the zone.
October 3 it trades over the hold day's high. Buy at market, 50.64. Stop 48.94, 3.4% away.
3.4% is wider than I like, so fewer shares. It hit 3R in 3 days, the best run in our set.

walkthroughs.title: MU, August 2025: the clean crossback that failed
steps: MU looked clean in August 2025. A pop on 1.3 times volume, a 3-day drift, then a hold day on August 18.
August 19: buy 123.70, stop 120.63, 2.5% away. The size came from that stop, so the loss is planned.
Next day it trades down to 113.46 and takes the stop. Take the loss. The stop did its job.
Weeks later it hit 3R and 5R without you. That's trading. A new buy needs a new hold day and trigger.

questions.q: What are you looking at here?
choices: The first pullback after the pop
Any dip in an uptrend
A bearish cross of the 9 and 20
Another pop back over the 20 EMA
questions.answer: The first pullback after the pop
questions.why: That's the EMA Crossback, the first pullback to the averages after the pop. This is LW in October 2018. It popped on a 3.4x volume earnings gap, then drifted 3 days onto the 9 EMA. We want the first one for a reason. Early in a new leg, the doubters sell the first dip. If the averages hold anyway, that selling went nowhere. LW traded over this bar's high next session at 73.21, stop 72.06, and hit 3R in 3 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: The crossback is the first pullback to the averages after the pop. The first one is the one we want.

wrong.Any dip in an uptrend: Only the first pullback after the pop counts. A stock that's been rising for weeks and dips is a different setup.
wrong.A bearish cross of the 9 and 20: Nothing crossed down. The 9 is still riding over the 20, which is what you want to see.
wrong.Another pop back over the 20 EMA: The pop already happened on the earnings gap. You're looking at the pullback after it.

questions.simple: It's the first pullback to the averages after the pop. If buyers hold them there, you've got your crossback.

reasons: rests on the held decision D-002 (Kell's definition against the house text)
the Kell quotes sit on archive pages the fetch tool could not open, so they are unverified

questions.story: This stock gapped up on earnings and popped back over its 9 and 20 EMA. Eight sessions later, after a 3-day drift, the last bar dips back to the 9 EMA.

deeper.counter: One thing on LW: the pullback came on heavy volume, 2.09x. We like to see volume dry up on the drift. Here it didn't, so I'd grade it a notch lower. It still worked.

questions.q: A crossback holds the averages while the 9 EMA is still above the 20 EMA.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The crossback is the pullback after the pop that holds the averages with the 9 still above the 20.
questions.lesson_line: Hold the averages with the 9 still over the 20.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We buy once price trades a few cents above the hold day's ___.
questions.answer: high
questions.why: High. The buy is a market order once price trades a few cents above the hold day's high. Entries are market orders, and the trigger is the high, not the close, the low or the open. Touching the averages is not a trigger either.
questions.lesson_line: Buy a few cents over the hold day's high, not the touch.
questions.simple: We buy at market once price trades a few cents over the hold day's high.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, entries are market orders)

questions.q: The stock popped, drifted back, and just touched its 9 and 20 EMA. You buy right there, on the touch.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. A touch is just price arriving. Nobody has proven anything yet. We wait for the hold day, a bar that dips into the averages and closes strong. Then we buy as price trades a few cents over its high. That wait pays. In our research a quarter of hold days broke their low before they ever triggered. Buy the touch and you eat every one of those.
questions.lesson_line: Don't buy the touch. Let the hold day close strong, then buy the break of its high.
questions.simple: False. A touch shows no buyers yet, so we wait for the hold day and buy the break of its high.

deeper.trap: The touch looks like the setup, and that's the trap. Nothing on the screen shows buyers yet. Kell says the same thing: always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in before making your trade.

reasons: Kell is the only web source; the named mistake is on our card

questions.q: Where does your stop go?
choices: A few cents under today's low
Right on today's low, to the penny
A few cents under the 20 EMA
Under the 200-day average
questions.answer: A few cents under today's low
questions.why: A few cents under the hold day's low. That's the low of the day (LOD) on the day buyers proved themselves. If price gets back under it, they didn't hold, and you want out. A few cents under, not right on it, so a quick tag of the low doesn't knock you out. On UAA the buy came next day at 40.82, stop 40.17. That's 1.6% of risk per share, so you get real size for a normal risk.
questions.lesson_line: Stop a few cents under the hold day's low. That's where the idea is wrong.

wrong.Right on today's low, to the penny: Too tight. Price tags an old low and bounces all the time. Give it a few cents under.
wrong.A few cents under the 20 EMA: The line isn't the stop. The hold day's low is, and it can sit above or below the 20.
wrong.Under the 200-day average: That's miles away. The 200-day tells you which stocks to buy, not where your stop goes.

questions.simple: Under the hold day's low. If price gets back under it, the buyers didn't hold and you're out small.

deeper.example: Kell does the same off support. He buys against the 10 or 20 EMA and uses that low as his stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3 and F62, stop first)

questions.story: A leader popped on 1.5x volume, then drifted back for 2 quiet sessions. Today it dipped to its 9 EMA and closed strong. You plan to buy over today's high.

questions.q: On this chart the 9 EMA has rolled under the 20. That alone says there's no reason to be long it.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A crossback needs the 9 riding above the 20. Here the 9 has rolled under it, so the short-term trend points down. This is AAPL in March 2022. It stopped out a crossback buy in February, and on this last bar it closed at 158.52, 5.93 under the 20 EMA. Yes, that last candle is a hammer. But a hammer sitting under the 9 and the 20, with the 50-day rolling over too, is a bounce, not a buy day. Let the 9 get back over the 20 first.
questions.lesson_line: 9 under the 20 means the short trend is down. No reason to be long.
questions.simple: True. With the 9 under the 20, the short trend is down, and we don't buy a trend that's pointed down.

reasons: the 9 and 20 pair is our house text while Kell uses 10 and 20 (D-021)

deeper.counter: In Kell's words, when the 10-day EMA is below the 20-day, there is no reason to be long the stock.

questions.q: In Kell's cycle, which stage comes right before the EMA Crossback?
choices: The Base n' Break
The Wedge Pop
The Exhaustion Extension
questions.answer: The Wedge Pop
questions.why: The Wedge Pop. After the Wedge Pop, the stock often tests its moving averages again, known as the EMA Crossback.
questions.lesson_line: Pop first, crossback second.

wrong.The Exhaustion Extension: That comes late in the cycle, and a Wedge Drop follows it, not a crossback.
wrong.The Base n' Break: That is another pullback after the crossback, so it comes later.

questions.q: Kell says a Wedge Pop is not just a cross of the averages. What should you focus on?
choices: Its price bars and its volume
A close above the 50-day
A weekly close over the 10-week
A new 52-week high first
questions.answer: Its price bars and its volume
questions.why: Price bars and volume. Kell says many traders wrongly think a Wedge Pop is simply about crossing the moving averages. He says to focus on price bars and volume.
questions.lesson_line: A pop is price bars and volume, not just a cross.

wrong.A close above the 50-day: A close over one line is the same trap. Kell says to look at price bars and volume.
wrong.A weekly close over the 10-week: Kell names price bars and volume, not a weekly line.
wrong.A new 52-week high first: The pop is the first rally back through the averages after a Reversal Extension, not a new high.

questions.simple: Price bars and volume. A cross of the averages alone is not enough.

reasons: one Kell article carries the key
the pop window is still open (D-076)

questions.q: One close back over the 20 EMA is already a crossback.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. One close back over the 20 EMA is a pop setting up, not a crossback. The crossback is the pullback after the pop.
questions.lesson_line: A pop first. The crossback is the pullback that follows.

questions.q: What makes this last bar a hold day?
choices: It dips to the averages, closes strong
It's the first close under the 20 EMA
It's the big up day of the pop
It touches the averages, that's it
questions.answer: It dips to the averages, closes strong
questions.why: It dips to the averages and closes strong. The low pushed through the 9 EMA and stopped just over the 20. Then buyers took it right back, and it closed near the high. That's a hammer, and an outside day too. A very good look. You want that close at or above the 20, in the top half of the range. CROX did this in April 2007 after 4 quiet days of drift. It traded over the high next day at 26.99, stop 25.86. That's 4.2%, wider than I like, but under 5% I'll take it with fewer shares.
questions.lesson_line: A hold day dips to the averages and closes strong. The close is the proof.

wrong.It's the first close under the 20 EMA: A close under the 20 means the line didn't hold that day. A hold day closes at or above it.
wrong.It's the big up day of the pop: The pop came first, on 1.3x volume. The hold day comes after, when the pullback reaches the averages.
wrong.It touches the averages, that's it: Touching is half of it. The close has to be strong too, or buyers never showed.

questions.simple: The low reaches the averages and the close is strong. That strong close shows buyers stepped in there.

deeper.trap: Touching the zone is only half of it. GE on the last day of 2025 reached the zone with its low, then closed in the bottom of its range. The close gave the day back, so it wasn't a hold day.

reasons: key rests on one proposed card line (x03), not an owner ruling
the hold day is a proposed criterion (xbk.hold_day)

questions.story: The pop came on 1.3x volume. Then 4 quiet days of drift brought the stock back down to its 9 and 20 EMA. Look at the last bar.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The hold day closes at or above the ___ EMA.
questions.why: 20. The hold day closes at or above the 20-day EMA, in the upper half of its range.
questions.lesson_line: The hold day closes at or above the 20 EMA.

questions.q: A crossback can come after a breakout from a base, not only after a Wedge Pop.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. What matters is a fresh leg up. A Wedge Pop starts one by turning a stock up out of a decline. A breakout over a base's pivot starts one too. Either way, the first rest back to the 9 and 20 EMA is the same test. Buyers defend the averages or they don't. So you trade it the same way: hold day, trigger over its high, stop under its low.
questions.lesson_line: A breakout can stand in for the pop. The first pullback after either one is the crossback.
questions.simple: True. A breakout starts a new leg just like a pop, so its first pullback to the averages is a crossback too.

reasons: one Kell line plus a proposed card line
the breakout stand-in is a proposed criterion

deeper.example: Kell posted DKNG pulling back to the crossback after a nice breakout. Same setup, different start.

questions.q: A clean crossback on a stock trading under its 200-day average is still a buy for us.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. We don't buy stocks under the 200-day. That's a hard line. Under it, the long trend is down, and our own market notes call it what it is: danger. A clean crossback shape doesn't change that. The only exception we make is indexes and the ETFs built to magnify them, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long. A crossback on a stock is neither, so the hold day has to close above the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: No stock longs under the 200-day. A pretty shape doesn't change that.
questions.simple: False. Under the 200-day is a hard no for stocks, however clean the crossback looks.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26, the 200-day line)

questions.q: The RS rating is the app's strength score. What is the lowest we accept on a crossback leader?
choices: An RS rating of 50
An RS rating of 70
An RS rating of 80
An RS rating of 95
questions.answer: An RS rating of 80
questions.why: An RS rating of 80, in a strong group. The RS rating is the app's score of how strong a stock has been against others. A crossback bets that a strong stock will use its averages as a springboard, as Kell puts it. A weaker stock has less pull, so 50 or 70 is not enough. 95 asks for more than the rule needs.
questions.lesson_line: We buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in a strong group.

wrong.An RS rating of 50: Our rule asks for an RS rating of 80 or more, not 50.
wrong.An RS rating of 70: Our rule asks for an RS rating of 80 or more, not 70.
wrong.An RS rating of 95: The floor is 80, so 95 asks for more than the rule needs.

questions.simple: 80 or more. We want strong stocks, because a strong stock tends to spring off its averages.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C31, RS 80 or more)

questions.q: Bought at 96.51, stop at 94.17 (1R is the gap between them). Where is 3R?
questions.why: $103.53. One R is the fill minus the stop: 96.51 - 94.17. Add three of those to the fill: 96.51 + 3 x (96.51 - 94.17) = 103.53. 3R is a measuring stick, not an order to sell. The first sell is a judgment.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. It is a yardstick, not a sell order.
questions.simple: 3R is the fill plus three times the gap down to the stop, which is 103.53 here. It is a measuring stick.

reasons: computed key (3R price)
the first sell is the owner's D-013 judgment, not a fixed 3R sale

wrong.$101.19: Counted 3R up from the stop, which is only two R above the fill.
wrong.$99.51: Added three dollars to the fill. 3R is three times the risk, not three dollars.
wrong.$105.87: Added four R, counting the fill as the first one.

questions.story: Bought on the trigger day.

questions.q: How far away is that stop, in percent?
questions.why: 3.6%. Take the gap and divide by your fill: (116.55 - 112.39) / 116.55 = 3.6%. That's wider than the 1 to 3% I like. But I'll take anything up to 5%, so this one's fine. The cost of a wider stop is fewer shares, not more risk. This is HOOD in September 2025, and it hit 3R in 6 days.
questions.lesson_line: Know your stop in percent before you buy. 1 to 3% is ideal, up to 5% is fine.
questions.simple: The stop is 3.6% under your fill. Wider than we like, but under 5%, so you just buy fewer shares.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A13, about 3%) and is tied to the pending D-005
fixed before (the old why leaned on size down past 3%)

wrong.4.2%: That's the dollar gap read as a percent. Divide the gap by your fill.
wrong.0.36%: Slipped a decimal place. Recheck where the point goes.
wrong.96.4%: That's the stop as a share of the fill. You want the gap between them.

questions.story: You bought the trigger at 116.55. Your stop sits a few cents under the hold day's low, at 112.39.

questions.q: How many shares do you buy?
questions.answer: 129 shares
questions.why: 129 shares. Start with what you're willing to lose: 90,000 x 0.6% is 540. Then the risk per share, 116.55 - 112.39. Divide the first by the second and round down: 129. Now if it stops you out, you lose about 540, the 0.6% you planned. That's the whole point. The stop sets the share count, so every loss is one you already signed up for.
questions.lesson_line: Dollars at risk divided by risk per share, rounded down. The stop sets the size.
questions.simple: Dollars at risk divided by the gap to your stop, rounded down. A stop-out then costs just the 0.6% you planned.

reasons: computed key (shares from risk)
rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, size from the stop)

choices: 151 shares
1,298 shares
772 shares
129 shares

wrong.151 shares: You divided the dollars by the stop's percent. Divide by the dollars per share instead.
wrong.772 shares: That puts the whole account in this stock. It ignores the stop.
wrong.1,298 shares: Ten times too many. The risk got typed one decimal place too big.

questions.story: You bought the trigger at 116.55 with your stop at 112.39. Your account is 90,000, and you risk 0.6% on this one, 540 dollars. The position cap isn't an issue here.

questions.q: A hold day's high is 64.00, its low 61.00, its close 63.40. How far up its range did it close, in percent (0 is the low, 100 the high)?
questions.why: 80%. The close above the low is 63.4 - 61. The range is 64 - 61. So (63.4 - 61) / (64 - 61) x 100 = 80%. That is in the upper half, where a hold day must close.
questions.lesson_line: A strong hold day closes in the upper half of its range.
questions.simple: The close is 80% of the way up the day's range, so it sits in the upper half.

reasons: computed key
the hold day is a proposed criterion (xbk.hold_day)

wrong.99%: Divided the close by the high. That ignores the low.
wrong.20%: Measured down from the high instead of up from the low.
wrong.3.8%: Divided by the close, not by the day's range.

questions.q: The 20 EMA is 100.00 and the hold day's low is 99.20. How far under the 20 EMA is the low, in percent?
questions.why: 0.8%. The low is under the 20 EMA by (100.00 - 99.20) / 100.00 x 100 = 0.8%. That is inside the zone, which runs down to about 1% under the 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: The zone reaches about 1% under the 20 EMA. Measure it.
questions.simple: The low is 0.8% under the 20 EMA, which is inside the zone that ends about 1% under it.

deeper.counter: The zone is a range, not a single line. It runs from the 9 EMA down to about 1% under the 20 EMA. A deeper undercut falls outside it. Another hold day had its low 2.1% under the 20 EMA, so it was outside.

reasons: computed key
the zone depth is a proposed criterion (xbk.depth)

wrong.99.2%: Gave the low as a share of the 20 EMA, not how far under it sits.
wrong.8%: A decimal slip. The low is under one percent below the line.

questions.q: Keep the alert, or drop it?
choices: Keep it, the high may still break
Keep it a few more days
Drop it, the setup's gone stale
Buy the break at half size
questions.answer: Drop it, the setup's gone stale
questions.why: Drop it. A hold day is proof buyers showed up on that day. Two weeks of nothing since, and that proof is old. The stock may still go, but it's a different picture now. The old low may not be the right stop anymore either. Wait for a fresh hold day. That gives you a fresh low to risk against and a fresh trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A hold day that never triggers goes stale. Drop it and wait for a fresh one.

wrong.Keep it, the high may still break: It might. But a break two weeks later isn't a trigger off this hold day anymore. Start over with a fresh one.
wrong.Keep it a few more days: More waiting doesn't freshen it up. It's already stale.
wrong.Buy the break at half size: Half size doesn't fix a stale setup. Your size comes from a stop under a fresh hold day's low.

questions.story: The hold day printed two weeks ago. Since then the stock has chopped just under its high and never traded through it. Your alert is still set.
questions.simple: Drop it. After two weeks with no break, the proof of buyers is old, so wait for a fresh hold day.

deeper.example: Say Monday was the hold day and nothing trades over Monday's high all week. By the next Monday that low and that proof don't describe the stock anymore. A new hold day gives you a new low for the stop. Kell's line fits: wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in.

reasons: key rests on one proposed card line (x08)
the 3-session window is tied to the pending D-003 (trigger)

questions.q: Do you buy tomorrow's break of the high?
choices: Yes, the hold day is clean
Yes, but only at half size
No, the report is too close
No, the hold day is too weak
questions.answer: No, the report is too close
questions.why: No. We don't make a new buy in the 3 days before a report. The reason is the gap. A report can open the stock way under your stop, and no stop catches an overnight gap. So your planned small loss turns into a big one. Half size still carries that gap. Let the report pass, then look for the next setup. We only hold through a report when the trade's already up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 days before a report. A stop can't catch the gap.

wrong.Yes, but only at half size: Half size still sits in front of the gap. No new buy this close to a report.
wrong.Yes, the hold day is clean: Clean doesn't help if the report gaps it through your stop. The calendar says no.
wrong.No, the hold day is too weak: The hold day closed strong. The report is the problem.

questions.story: The hold day closed strong today. The company reports earnings in 3 sessions.
questions.simple: No. A report can gap the stock right through your stop, and no stop catches an overnight gap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22, no new buy within 3 days of a report)

questions.q: What do you call this pullback?
choices: EMA Crossback, the first retest
20 EMA Pullback, an old rising 20
Wedge Pop, the first close over
Breakout, a push to new highs
questions.answer: EMA Crossback, the first retest
questions.why: EMA Crossback. Count the rests since the turn. The pop came nine sessions ago, and today's the first time it's come back to the averages. That first test is where the doubters sell and the averages hold or they don't. This is SNPS in June 2021. It drifted five sessions onto the 20, then traded over the high at 252.62 with a stop at 247.84. It made a new high within two weeks.
questions.lesson_line: First test after the pop is the crossback. A tap of an old rising 20 is the pullback.

wrong.20 EMA Pullback, an old rising 20: That's a tap of a 20 that's been rising for weeks. This stock just came out of a three-month correction.
wrong.Wedge Pop, the first close over: The pop was nine sessions ago. You're looking at the pullback after it.
wrong.Breakout, a push to new highs: It's testing its averages, not pushing to a new high.

questions.story: A three-month correction ended nine sessions ago with a pop on 1.7x volume. It has held over its 9 and 20 EMA since. Today it dips back to them and closes strong.
questions.simple: It's the first pullback to the averages since the pop, so it's a crossback, not a 20 EMA Pullback.

reasons: rests on the held decision D-002 (crossback against the 20 EMA Pullback)

questions.q: What stage is this?
choices: An EMA Crossback, the first retest
A Wedge Pop, the first reclaim
A Base n' Break, a later rest
A Wedge Drop, a break lower
questions.answer: A Wedge Pop, the first reclaim
questions.why: A Wedge Pop. It's the first rally back through the averages after the decline. Nothing has pulled back yet, so there's no crossback to buy. The crossback is the pullback that comes after this. You want to see the bar close over both lines with real volume, and here it did on 1.7x. Put it on your radar and wait for the first pullback. SNPS gave it nine sessions later.
questions.lesson_line: The pop is the first move back over the averages. The crossback is the first pullback after it.

wrong.A Wedge Drop, a break lower: A Wedge Drop breaks down through the averages after a blow-off. This stock is turning up.
wrong.An EMA Crossback, the first retest: Nothing has pulled back yet. You're looking at the reclaim itself.
wrong.A Base n' Break, a later rest: That's a later rest, after the crossback.

questions.story: After a three-month correction, the stock closes back over its 9 and 20 EMA on 1.7x volume.
questions.simple: It's the pop itself, the first move back over the averages. The crossback is the pullback that comes after.

deeper.counter: Kell's point on the pop: many traders think it's just a cross of the averages. Read the price bars and the volume instead. Later, if the same stock pulls back and holds with the 9 over the 20, that pullback is the crossback.

reasons: the whole unit rests on Kell's definition (D-002)
the pop window is open (D-076)

questions.q: What's the right name for this rest?
choices: EMA Crossback, the first rest
Base n' Break, a later rest
Wedge Pop, the move before
Exhaustion Extension, a climax
questions.answer: Base n' Break, a later rest
questions.why: Base n' Break. Count the rests. It already came back to the averages once since the pop, so this one's the second. The crossback is only the first. Kell calls a later rest the Base n' Break. I grade it lower, because in our own test the first crossback in a leg did better than the second. This is AMZN in November 2023. The candle itself is a good one, a doji with a long lower wick that closed right at the high. It worked, but it wasn't a crossback entry.
questions.lesson_line: The crossback is the first rest after the pop. The second one is a Base n' Break.

wrong.EMA Crossback, the first rest: The crossback is the first rest. You're on the second.
wrong.Wedge Pop, the move before: The pop came sixteen sessions ago, before the first rest.
wrong.Exhaustion Extension, a climax: That's a blow-off far above the 9 EMA. This stock is resting at its averages.

questions.story: A hold day just closed. The stock popped sixteen sessions ago and has already pulled into its averages once. Today it pulls back into them again.
questions.simple: It already rested at the averages once, so this second rest is a Base n' Break, not the crossback.

reasons: tied to the pending D-026 (a second pullback: Base n' Break or a graded-lower crossback)
fixed before (the old why said graded lower)

questions.q: A close under the 20 EMA on above-average volume ends the setup before the trigger.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A close under the 20 EMA on above-average volume ends the setup before the trigger. That is the opposite of a hold day, which must close at or above the 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: A heavy close under the 20 EMA ends the idea.
questions.simple: Yes. A close under the 20 EMA on above-average volume ends the idea before we buy.

reasons: a proposed card line with no web source

questions.q: Is this a crossback buy?
choices: No, the 9 is still under the 20
Yes, if the stop is tight
Yes, it's back over its 50-day line
No, it needs a gap up first
questions.answer: No, the 9 is still under the 20
questions.why: No. Look at the two short averages. The 9 is at 52.10, under the 20 at 52.80. So the short-term trend is still down. A crossback needs the 9 riding above the 20, with price holding them. Getting back over the 50-day is a start, but it's not this setup. Let the 9 cross back over the 20 first. Then see if you get a real pop and a pullback.
questions.lesson_line: A crossback needs the 9 above the 20. Under it, there's no reason to be long.

wrong.Yes, if the stop is tight: A tight stop doesn't change the trend. The 9 is still under the 20.
wrong.Yes, it's back over its 50-day line: The 50-day is a start. The short averages still point down.
wrong.No, it needs a gap up first: A gap isn't required. The problem is the 9 sitting under the 20.

questions.story: A stock popped weeks ago, then closed under its 50-day for nine sessions. Today it closed back above it. The 9 EMA is at 52.10 and the 20 EMA at 52.80.
questions.simple: No. The 9 is under the 20, so the short trend is still down, and a crossback needs it pointed up.

reasons: the 9 and 20 pair is our house text while Kell uses 10 and 20 (D-021)

deeper.counter: Kell's version: when the fast average is under the 20-day, there is no reason to be long the stock.

questions.q: Is this a crossback?
choices: No, it never came back to them
Yes, the run was the pop
Yes, a tight drift up there is enough
No, crossbacks need a pole
questions.answer: No, it never came back to them
questions.why: No, not yet anyway. A crossback is a test of the averages, and this stock hasn't come back to them. Nobody has shown you they'll buy at the 9 and 20. Tight action up high is nice, but it's a different setup. Keep it on your radar. If it drifts down into the zone around the 9 and 20 and holds, then you've got your crossback.
questions.lesson_line: No touch of the 9 and 20, no crossback. Keep it on your radar.

wrong.Yes, the run was the pop: Maybe it was. But the pullback has to reach the averages to be a crossback.
wrong.Yes, a tight drift up there is enough: Tight only counts if it drifts down into the 9 and 20 zone.
wrong.No, crossbacks need a pole: No pole needed. The problem is it never reached the averages.

questions.story: A stock pops, then hovers for six sessions well above its 9 and 20 EMA. It never touches either line.
questions.simple: No. A crossback tests the averages, and this one never came back to them, so keep watching.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (x27) and the pending bull-flag pole option
fixed before (the pole was raised to 32% to clear the 30% option)

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Stand aside until a new hold day
Buy anyway on the old trigger
Buy the dip under the low
Keep the alert on the old hold day high
questions.answer: Stand aside until a new hold day
questions.why: Stand aside. Your whole trade was built on that low. It was the proof buyers held the line, and it was where your stop would sit. It just broke before you ever got in, so the setup's off. In our research a quarter of hold days did exactly this before triggering. Waiting for the trigger kept you out of every one. Now watch for a new hold day.
questions.lesson_line: Hold day low breaks before the trigger, the setup's off. Wait for a new one.

wrong.Buy anyway on the old trigger: The hold day failed. Its high isn't a trigger anymore.
wrong.Buy the dip under the low: That's buying a broken setup cheaper. Wait for a new hold day.
wrong.Keep the alert on the old hold day high: Once the low breaks, the old high means nothing. Reset on a new hold day.

questions.story: Yesterday was the hold day. This morning, before it ever traded over the high, the stock breaks under the hold day's low.
questions.simple: Stand aside. The low that proved buyers held just broke, so wait for a new hold day.

reasons: key rests on one proposed card line (x07)
the low-break rule is a proposed criterion (xbk.inv_low_break)

questions.q: What now?
choices: Buy the next day's high anyway
Wait one more day for the trigger
The setup is off
questions.answer: The setup is off
questions.why: The setup is off. A close under the 20 EMA on above-average volume ends it before the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A heavy close under the 20 EMA ends the idea.

wrong.Buy the next day's high anyway: The setup ended before any trigger.
wrong.Wait one more day for the trigger: The close under the 20 EMA on volume ends it.

questions.story: The hold day looked good. Then the stock closes under its 20 EMA on above-average volume.

questions.q: Kell buys in pieces. For us, adding a second piece after the crossback buy is part of the plan.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Kell buys in pieces, and it works for him. We don't. We buy the full size once, at one price, with one stop. Here's why. Your stop sets your size. A second piece bought higher sits farther from that same stop, so it adds risk you never planned. Adding to a working winner happens, but rarely, and only as a feel call. Learn from his read of the chart. Trade our plan.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop, full size. Adding is never the plan.
questions.simple: False. We buy once with one stop, because a second piece bought higher adds risk you didn't plan.

deeper.trap: The trap is borrowing a great trader's method whole. Kell also staggers his stops under the 10 and 20 EMA. We don't. Take his chart reads and keep our plan.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5)

questions.q: What does our plan say?
choices: Add a second piece on the clear
Move the stop under the new low
No add; one price, one stop
questions.answer: No add; one price, one stop
questions.why: No add. A full new entry at one price with one stop: no pilot, no add on follow-through, no staggered stops. Adding or scaling in is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop. Kell may add; we do not.

wrong.Add a second piece on the clear: That is Kell's way, not our plan.
wrong.Move the stop under the new low: The stop only moves up on the plan's own steps.

questions.story: You bought the crossback over the hold day's high at 50.64. Two days later it clears the pop high.

questions.q: Is this a crossback you buy?
choices: No, a Wedge Drop is more likely
Yes, buy it on the touch
Yes, it's still the first pullback
No, it's a Base n' Break
questions.answer: No, a Wedge Drop is more likely
questions.why: No. Look at what came before. This isn't a fresh leg off a low. It's the pullback after a blow-off. In Kell's cycle the stage after an Exhaustion Extension is the Wedge Drop, the first break down through the averages. After a run like that, the first pullback is more likely the start of a top than a new leg. I'd let it go and wait for a new base and a new pop.
questions.lesson_line: After an Exhaustion Extension, look for a Wedge Drop, not a crossback.

wrong.Yes, buy it on the touch: Buying the touch is a mistake on any crossback, and this isn't one.
wrong.Yes, it's still the first pullback: First pullback after a blow-off, not after a pop. Different stage.
wrong.No, it's a Base n' Break: A Base n' Break is a later rest in a healthy leg. This came after a climax.

questions.story: A stock ran far above its 9 EMA in a blow-off, an Exhaustion Extension. Now it pulls back into its averages.
questions.simple: No. After a blow-off run, the next stage is more often a break lower than a new leg up.

reasons: a proposed card line built on Kell's cycle

questions.q: Do you buy it?
choices: No, it's under the 200-day
Yes, half size with a stop
Yes, the gap makes it parabolic
No, wait for a close over the 50
questions.answer: No, it's under the 200-day
questions.why: No. It closed 6% under the 200-day, and we don't buy stocks down there. Doesn't matter how textbook the shape is. Under the 200-day the long trend is down, and our own market notes call it danger. The gap-up pop doesn't make it a parabolic long either. The one exception we make is for indexes and the ETFs built to magnify them. Pass, and look again when it's back over the line.
questions.lesson_line: A crossback under the 200-day is a pass. Every time.

wrong.Yes, half size with a stop: Size doesn't lift the rule. Under the 200-day is a no for stocks.
wrong.Yes, the gap makes it parabolic: A gap-up pop isn't a parabolic long, and stocks get no exception anyway.
wrong.No, wait for a close over the 50: The 50 isn't the issue. The 200-day is.

questions.story: After a gap-up Wedge Pop, a textbook first crossback prints its hold day. That hold day closes 6% under the 200-day.
questions.simple: No. It's under the 200-day, and we don't buy stocks there, however clean it looks.

deeper.trap: The gap-up pop doesn't make this an exception. Only indexes and the ETFs built to magnify them get bought under the 200-day. That's on a reversal extension or a parabolic long. A stock doesn't get that pass, however textbook it looks.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26, the 200-day line)

questions.q: How does the market cue grade it?
choices: Higher; the stock is a leader
Lower; these setups fail most
The same; the index is ignored
No grade; the index is a gate
questions.answer: Lower; these setups fail most
questions.why: Lower. Crossbacks taken with the Nasdaq under its 20 EMA fail most, and the card lists that as a lower-grade cue. It is a cue, not a gate, and the stop is still the exit.
questions.lesson_line: Watch the index. Crossbacks fail most with the Nasdaq under its 20 EMA.

wrong.Higher; the stock is a leader: Crossbacks taken with the Nasdaq under its 20 EMA fail most, so this does not raise the grade.
wrong.The same; the index is ignored: Kell sizes down or stands aside during index corrections below the 20 EMA.
wrong.No grade; the index is a gate: The card calls the index a cue, not a gate. It lowers the grade but does not block the trade.

questions.story: A leader gives a clean crossback. The Nasdaq 100 is trading under its own 20-day EMA.
questions.simple: The grade goes lower, because crossbacks taken with the Nasdaq under its 20 EMA fail most.

deeper.counter: The card's cue reads two ways: the Nasdaq is not below its 20-day EMA, or a market Wedge Pop has just happened. The first is a cue, not a gate. Kell sizes down or stands aside in index corrections.

reasons: a proposed card cue backed by Kell's advice to size down in corrections

questions.q: Do you take it?
choices: Pass, Orange is for A+ setups
Take it, full size, it's clean
Take it, half size, it's a B
Pass, Orange means all cash
questions.answer: Pass, Orange is for A+ setups
questions.why: Pass. In an Orange market, setups fail more often, because the market isn't backing them. So I only want my very best ideas, the A+ setups. You've got a B. Half size doesn't turn a B into an A+. It just means a smaller loss on a trade you didn't need. Keep it on your radar. If the market turns Yellow or Green, it's a different call.
questions.lesson_line: Orange market, A+ only. Let the market earn your exposure.

wrong.Take it, full size, it's clean: Clean isn't enough in Orange. Full risk is for a Green market.
wrong.Take it, half size, it's a B: Smaller doesn't fix the grade. In Orange I only want A+.
wrong.Pass, Orange means all cash: Close, but mostly cash is Red. Orange still allows an A+.

questions.story: The app's market filter reads Orange: the market's under pressure, one step from Red. A leader sets up a clean crossback. You'd grade it a B, not an A+, our cleanest kind.
questions.simple: Pass. In an Orange market I only want A+ setups, and this one's a B.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A10 and F65, the market reading as a guide)

deeper.counter: Kell does the same thing his way. He sizes down or stands aside when the index corrects below its 20 EMA.

questions.q: Is it a valid hold day?
choices: No; a weak close
Yes; the low reached the zone
Yes; it later reached 3R
questions.answer: No; a weak close
questions.why: No. The hold day closed in the lower 3% of its range, not the upper half. The low reached the zone but the close gave it back.
questions.lesson_line: A hold day needs a strong close, not just a touch.

wrong.Yes; the low reached the zone: The close matters as much as the low.
wrong.Yes; it later reached 3R: That was luck, not the setup.

questions.story: GE touched the zone, but the hold day closed in the lower 3% of its range.

questions.q: Which gate fails?
choices: The close was too weak to hold
The dip under the line was too deep
The 9 EMA crossed under the 20 EMA
The hold day was not the first pullback
questions.answer: The dip under the line was too deep
questions.why: The depth. The hold day's low sat 2.1% under the 20 EMA, and the zone runs down to about 1% under it. A deeper undercut is a different shape, an Undercut and Rally if anything. It did close back over the line.
questions.lesson_line: The zone ends about 1% under the 20 EMA.

wrong.The close was too weak to hold: The story says it closed back over the 20 EMA. The problem is the depth of the low.
wrong.The 9 EMA crossed under the 20 EMA: Nothing in the story says the averages crossed.
wrong.The hold day was not the first pullback: Nothing in the story says it was a second pullback. The gate that fails is the depth of the low.

questions.story: A hold day just closed. It closed back over the 20 EMA, but its low sat 2.1% under the line.
questions.simple: The low went 2.1% under the 20 EMA, but the zone ends about 1% under it.

deeper.example: AMAT, 2023-08-28: the low sat 2.1% under the 20 EMA against a rule of at most 1%. It was stopped, best run 2.27R. CLS undercut by only 0.6% and closed back over the line, and it reached 3R in 3 days.

reasons: the 1% depth line is a proposed criterion
a number that the owner may change

questions.q: In our scan of daily bars, most crossbacks reached 3R before they hit the stop.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False, and it's not close. Only 28.9% reached 3R before the stop, and 17.6% reached 5R. Most didn't. So this setup doesn't pay by being right a lot. It pays through a few big winners. That's why the stop and the size matter so much. Keep the losses small and planned, and the winners do the work. A loss at the stop is the system working.
questions.lesson_line: Most crossbacks stop out. A few big winners pay for them, so keep every loss small.
questions.simple: False. Fewer than three in ten reached 3R first, so a few big winners pay for all the rest.

deeper.counter: Do not read 82.6% as the loss rate. It counts any trade that touched the stop within 60 sessions, even one that reached 3R first. The 28.9% and the 82.6% overlap, since together they are more than all the trades.

reasons: one cited fact only (d24)
a number from our own scan, which changes with the data

questions.q: Your normal size doesn't fit that stop. What do you do?
choices: Keep the stop, buy fewer shares
Pull the stop in to 3%, same size
Buy half now, half on a dip
Skip it, the stop is over 3%
questions.answer: Keep the stop, buy fewer shares
questions.why: Keep the stop and buy fewer shares. 48.94 is where the chart says you're wrong, a few cents under the hold day's low. From 50.64 that's 3.4%. Wider than the 1 to 3% I like, but 3.5% is good and I'll go up to 5%. The size comes from the stop, never the other way. Pull it in to fit more shares and normal noise knocks you out of a good trade. This was CLS in October 2024, and it hit 3R in 3 days.
questions.lesson_line: Wider stop, fewer shares. Never pull the stop in to fit the size.

wrong.Pull the stop in to 3%, same size: That's moving the stop to fit the size. Normal noise takes you out, and the stop means nothing.
wrong.Buy half now, half on a dip: We buy once, at one price, with one stop. No buying it in pieces.
wrong.Skip it, the stop is over 3%: 3.4% is fine. We take stops up to 5%. A wider honest stop just gets fewer shares.

questions.story: You're buying the trigger at 50.64. The hold day's low puts your stop at 48.94, 3.4% away. Your risk percent is set.
questions.simple: Keep the stop where the chart puts it and buy fewer shares. The stop sets the size, never the other way.

deeper.example: Work it with the same risk in dollars. A 3.4% stop buys fewer shares than a tighter one would. The loss if it's wrong stays the same.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3 and A5) and is tied to the pending D-005
fixed before (the old why leaned on size down past 3%)

questions.q: You're stopped out. What now?
choices: Take the loss, wait for a new setup
Buy it right back, it looked so clean
Wait three days, then buy again
Lower the stop, give it room
questions.answer: Take the loss, wait for a new setup
questions.why: Take the loss and wait for a new setup. The stop did its job. Your size came from it, so this loss was planned before you bought. This is MU in August 2025. It looked clean and simply failed. A re-buy needs a new hold day and a new trigger, as a brand new trade. Here's the part that stings. MU hit 3R and 5R weeks later without us. The stop was still right.
questions.lesson_line: After a stop-out, wait for a new hold day and a new trigger. Then it's a new trade.

wrong.Wait three days, then buy again: Time isn't a trigger. Wait for the chart to give you a new one.
wrong.Buy it right back, it looked so clean: Looking clean is how you got stopped. A re-buy needs a new hold day and a new trigger.
wrong.Lower the stop, give it room: A stop only moves up. Giving it room is how small losses get big.

questions.story: A pop on 1.3x volume, a 3-day drift and a clean hold day. You bought at 123.70 with the stop at 120.63. The next session it fell through the stop.
questions.simple: Take the loss and wait for a new setup. The loss was planned, and buying right back is just guessing.

deeper.trap: The hardest part is the shakeout. MU later reached 3R (132.91) and 5R (139.05) without us, so the stop felt wrong. It wasn't. A new buy needs a new hold day and a new trigger. And it's at most 3 tries a week, 6 a month.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21)

questions.q: On one stock we take at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. On one stock we take at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month. A try after a stop-out is a new trade, so it needs a new trigger and every rule.
questions.lesson_line: Cap the tries. A new try needs a new trigger.
questions.simple: Yes. We cap one stock at 3 tries a week and 6 a month.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E56)

questions.q: Which line do you trail what's left with?
choices: The 9 EMA
The 20 EMA
The 50-day
The 200-day
questions.answer: The 9 EMA
questions.why: The 9 EMA. A fast mover rides the 9, so that's the line I trail it with. You sell what's left on a close below it. A steadier stock that keeps tapping the 20 gets the 20 instead. The point of a trail is to stay in while the trend holds and get out when it breaks. A fast stock that closes under the 9 has broken its own rhythm.
questions.lesson_line: Fast movers trail the 9 EMA. Steadier ones trail the 20.

wrong.The 50-day: Way too loose for a fast crossback. You'd hand back most of the move.
wrong.The 200-day: That line tells you which stocks to buy, not how to trail a winner.
wrong.The 20 EMA: That's the trail for a steadier stock. On a fast mover you'd give back too much by the 20.

questions.simple: The 9 EMA. A fast mover rides the 9, and a close under it says the run is breaking.

reasons: one cited fact only (h21)
rests on the owner's rulebook (E52) and is tied to the pending D-019 (exit management)

questions.story: You sold some of your crossback winner into a fast 5-day push. Now you want to trail the rest. It's a fast mover, riding well above its 20 EMA.

questions.q: What's the plan?
choices: Sell it and free up the money
Add more while it's quiet
Hold it, the hold day was clean
Move the stop up to entry
questions.answer: Sell it and free up the money
questions.why: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days gets sold. A crossback should work early. The whole idea is that buyers show up at the averages and push it. If they haven't in 10 days, the idea isn't working, even if the stop hasn't hit. That money can go to a setup that's actually moving. Adding to a flat trade is never on the table, and breakeven is a 2R to 5R move.
questions.lesson_line: Under 1R after 10 days, sell it and put the money to work.

wrong.Add more while it's quiet: Adding to a trade that isn't working just ties up more money. One price, one stop.
wrong.Hold it, the hold day was clean: The time stop doesn't care how clean the start was. It's day 10 and under 1R.
wrong.Move the stop up to entry: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, and this is 0.6R. The time stop sells it anyway.

questions.story: You bought a crossback and it's drifted sideways since. Day 10 just closed, and the trade is up only 0.6R.
questions.simple: Sell it. A crossback should work early, and money stuck in a flat trade could be working somewhere else.

reasons: one cited fact only (h15)
rests on the owner's rulebook (C33, the time stop)

questions.q: What do you do about your first sell?
choices: Judge it, there's no fixed sell
Sell a third at the open, by rule
Wait for the close, sell a third
Sell at 5R, by rule, not before
questions.answer: Judge it, there's no fixed sell
questions.why: Judge it. There's no rule that says sell a third at 3R. I very rarely sell on day 1, and I wait until day 3 at the earliest most of the time. This setup pays through a few big winners. A gap up on day 1 is what a big winner looks like early. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or around 5 to 10R, is often best. Selling some into a big gap is a choice you can make. It's not an order.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is judgment, often into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. Not a fixed third at 3R.

wrong.Sell a third at the open, by rule: There's no fixed third. Selling some into a gap is a judgment call.
wrong.Sell at 5R, by rule, not before: 5R is often a good spot, but it's judgment, not a fixed level.
wrong.Wait for the close, sell a third: Waiting for the close doesn't make it a rule. Still a judgment.

questions.story: You bought at 116.55 with the stop at 112.39. Next morning the stock opens at 130.00, above 3R at 129.03.
questions.simple: Judge it. The big winners pay for everything, so I rarely sell on the first day, even into a gap.

reasons: rests on the owner's ruling D-013 (the first sell is a judgment)

questions.q: What decides your exit?
choices: The first 30-minute low, out past 2R
Hold it and wait for it to come back
Your old stop at 120.63 still rules
The day's close sets the new stop
questions.answer: The first 30-minute low, out past 2R
questions.why: The gap rule. A stop can't catch an overnight gap, so 120.63 is already behind you. You let the first 30 minutes show the real low, and that low is your new stop. With one cap: if those 30 minutes put you past a 2R loss, you get out. Work it here. From 123.70 down to 113.46 is more than three times your 3.07 of risk. That's well past 2R, so you sell.
questions.lesson_line: Gap through your stop: the first 30-minute low is the new stop. Past 2R, get out.

wrong.The day's close sets the new stop: The first 30 minutes decide, not the close.
wrong.Hold it and wait for it to come back: Hoping isn't a plan. The gap rule decides, and here it says out.
wrong.Your old stop at 120.63 still rules: The stock opened through it. That stop can't fill there anymore.

questions.story: You bought at 123.70 with the stop at 120.63, so 1R is 3.07. The stock gaps down hard. Say its first 30-minute low is 113.46.
questions.simple: A gap jumps your old stop. The first 30 minutes set the new one, and past a 2R loss you're out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)

questions.q: How do you play it?
choices: Buy at market, stop under its low
Wait for a full close over the high
Buy half now, add on strength
Buy at market, stop at entry
questions.answer: Buy at market, stop under its low
questions.why: Buy it at market, right as it trades through the high. Your stop goes a few cents under the hold day's low. The break of the high is buyers coming back, and that's your trigger. I don't wait for a close. By then it can be well past the trigger, and you're chasing. This is NET in November 2023. The buy came at 63.34 with the stop at 61.31, about 3.2% away. That's a touch wider than the 1 to 3% I like, but well inside 5%. The trigger day itself ran past 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Buy it as it trades through the hold day's high. Stop a few cents under the low.

wrong.Wait for a full close over the high: The trigger is price trading through the high, not a close. Waiting can cost you the move.
wrong.Buy half now, add on strength: We buy the full size once, at one price, with one stop. No starter piece.
wrong.Buy at market, stop at entry: A stop at entry is breakeven, and that comes later, from 2R to 5R. Your first stop goes under the low.

questions.story: A leader popped on strong volume, then drifted back for three sessions. The hold day closed strong over the 20 EMA. Next morning the stock trades a few cents over the hold day's high.
questions.simple: Buy at market over the hold day's high. That break shows buyers are back, and the stop goes under its low.

deeper.trap: The trap is the second piece. A clean trigger feels like a reason to buy half now and add later. We buy the full size at one price with one stop, and the stop sets the size.

reasons: the trigger shape waits on the owner (D-003)

questions.q: Is this still a good hold day?
choices: Yes, a small dip that closed back
No, any low under the 20 EMA fails
No, the stop would be too wide
Yes, even a close under is fine
questions.answer: Yes, a small dip that closed back
questions.why: Yes. The low poked 0.6% under the 20, and the close came right back over it, in the top half of the range. That's a nice tell. Sellers pushed it under the line and buyers took it back the same day. How deep is too deep is a judgment call, not a fixed number. A small undercut like this that closes back over is fine. You'll also see the 50-day still pointed down from the correction. That's normal this early in a new leg, and price is back over it. This was CLS in October 2024, the best run in our set.
questions.lesson_line: A small dip under the 20 that closes back over is still a hold.

wrong.No, any low under the 20 EMA fails: A small undercut that closes back over still holds. Depth is a judgment call.
wrong.No, the stop would be too wide: A wider stop just means fewer shares. It doesn't kill the hold day.
wrong.Yes, even a close under is fine: The close has to come back over the line. A close under means the line was lost.

questions.story: A hold day just closed after four quiet sessions. Its low dipped 0.6% under the 20 EMA. It closed back over the line, in the upper half of its range.
questions.simple: Yes. It dipped a little under the 20 and buyers took it back by the close, so it's a hold.

deeper.counter: A much deeper undercut is a different story. AMAT's hold day low sat 2.1% under the 20 EMA, and it was stopped after a best run of 2.27R. How deep is too deep stays a judgment call.

reasons: the zone depth is a proposed criterion (xbk.depth), not an owner ruling
tied to the pending D-005 through the stop-width wrong answer
fixed before (the old why leaned on size down past 3%)

questions.q: Does a low right on the 20 count?
choices: Yes, the low reached the zone
No, it has to pierce the line
No, it needs a gap down first
Yes, and the close doesn't matter
questions.answer: Yes, the low reached the zone
questions.why: Yes. The low only has to reach the zone, the area around the 9 and 20 EMA. Right on the 20 is in it. What it still needs is the strong close, because that's the proof buyers took the line. ALGN had both in February 2017: six sessions of drift, the low exactly on the 20, a strong close. It traded over the high at 96.51 with the stop at 94.17, 2.4% away.
questions.lesson_line: The low only has to reach the zone. The close still has to be strong.

wrong.No, it has to pierce the line: Reaching the line is enough. It doesn't have to poke through.
wrong.No, it needs a gap down first: The setup is a drift into the averages, not a gap down.
wrong.Yes, and the close doesn't matter: The close matters as much as the low. It has to be strong.

questions.story: The stock popped on 3.7x volume, then drifted six sessions. Today's low sat exactly on the 20 EMA, and it closed strong.
questions.simple: Yes. Reaching the zone is enough, as long as the close is strong and buyers took the line.

reasons: the zone depth is a proposed criterion
one dossier row backs the example

questions.q: Looking back, what warning did this one carry?
choices: It came late in its own run
The 9 crossed under the 20
The hold day had thin volume
It came too soon after the pop
questions.answer: It came late in its own run
questions.why: It came late in its own run. Sixteen sessions after the pop, after a long advance, a lot of the move is already behind it. I trust a late one less, and it gets a lower grade. But it's a warning, not a gate. Late ones still work sometimes, which is why the stop decides, not the calendar. This was LLY in September 2024. The stop did its job the next day, and the size kept the loss small.
questions.lesson_line: Late in a run is a warning, not a gate. The stop still decides.

wrong.The 9 crossed under the 20: The story doesn't say that. The averages weren't the issue.
wrong.The hold day had thin volume: The story doesn't say that. Quiet volume on a pullback is a plus anyway.
wrong.It came too soon after the pop: Sixteen sessions isn't soon. It's late.

questions.story: A hold day just closed, sixteen sessions after the pop and after a long advance. You bought the trigger, and the next day it hit the stop.
questions.simple: It came late in its own run. That's a warning that lowers the grade, not a rule that bans it.

deeper.trap: Kell warns against buying late in an uptrend, the same way he warns against shorting late in a downtrend. Still, one stop-out doesn't prove a rule. Lateness lowers the grade. The stop decides.

reasons: the pop window is still open (D-076)
'late fails most' is the card's line; our own scan did not confirm it

questions.q: Did that buy break our earnings rule?
choices: No, it was outside the window
Yes, any report nearby is a no
Yes, we only buy after reports
No, a stop covers report risk
questions.answer: No, it was outside the window
questions.why: No. The report came five sessions after the entry, and our rule is no new buys in the 3 days before a report. So it was a legal buy. The rule exists because a report can gap the stock right through your stop. Here it just got stopped the next day, a normal small loss. NFLX in April 2023 then reached 3R and 5R weeks later without us.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 days before a report. Five sessions out is fine.

wrong.Yes, any report nearby is a no: The window is 3 days. Five sessions out is outside it.
wrong.Yes, we only buy after reports: No rule says wait for the report. Just no new buys in the 3 days before it.
wrong.No, a stop covers report risk: Right call, wrong reason. A stop can't catch a gap. The timing made it fine.

questions.story: You bought a crossback trigger. The company's report came five sessions after your buy. The day after you bought, it hit your stop.
questions.simple: No. The report was five sessions out, past the 3 day window that guards against a gap through your stop.

deeper.counter: Had the report been due within 3 sessions, the buy would be off however clean the hold day. We hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: Which entry is this?
choices: A Wedge Pop
The EMA Crossback
A Base n' Break, graded lower
questions.answer: A Base n' Break, graded lower
questions.why: A Base n' Break, graded lower. It was the second pullback into the zone since the pop, so it is not this card's entry, even though it worked.
questions.lesson_line: A winner can still be the wrong card. Count the rests.

wrong.The EMA Crossback: The crossback is the first rest. This was the second.

questions.story: AMZN popped on 10-30. It pulled into its averages on 11-21 for the second time since the pop and then ran 9.94R.

questions.q: What do you do with it?
choices: Ignore it; only the stock matters
Skip it; the index is a hard gate
Treat the index cue as a grade cue
questions.answer: Treat the index cue as a grade cue
questions.why: Treat it as a grade cue, not a gate. Kell sizes down or stands aside during index corrections, and a market Wedge Pop is the best cue.
questions.lesson_line: The index cue is a cue. A weak index lowers the grade.

wrong.Skip it; the index is a hard gate: The card calls it a cue, not a gate.
wrong.Ignore it; only the stock matters: A weak index makes crossbacks fail more often.

questions.story: A clean crossback sets up on a leader while the Nasdaq sits just under its 20-day EMA.

questions.q: Where does your stop go?
choices: A few cents under the day's low
At breakeven, right at your buy
Under the 65-minute bar's low
Just under the 200-day line
questions.answer: A few cents under the day's low
questions.why: Same place as always, a few cents under the low of the day. Buying earlier on the hold day doesn't change where the idea fails. That's still the low where buyers stepped in at the averages. The 65-minute bar is just your entry timing. Breakeven comes later, somewhere from 2R to 5R, or at your first sell.
questions.lesson_line: An earlier entry keeps the same stop, a few cents under the day's low.

wrong.Just under the 200-day line: Way too far. The day's low is the stop.
wrong.At breakeven, right at your buy: Too early. Breakeven comes from 2R to 5R, or at the first sell.
wrong.Under the 65-minute bar's low: That bar is your entry timing, not where the idea fails. Use the day's low.

questions.story: You buy early, on the hold day itself, as the stock breaks its 65-minute high. The day's low is already in.
questions.simple: Same stop, under the day's low. Buying earlier doesn't change where the idea fails.

reasons: the advanced version is a proposed card line

questions.q: Is that a chase, or do you buy it?
choices: Buy it, it's inside the 4% limit
Skip it, any gap over is a chase
Wait for a dip back to 424.70
Buy it, but at half size
questions.answer: Buy it, it's inside the 4% limit
questions.why: Buy it. 429.33 over a 424.70 trigger is 1.1%. We don't buy more than 4% over the buy point, and this is well inside that. A gap isn't a chase by itself. The real cost of chasing is size. Your stop stays under the hold day's low, so a higher fill means fewer shares. At 1.1% that cost is tiny. One honest flaw: it's a tad extended from the 50-day. But the hold day's low sat right on the 9 EMA, so the stop is still close. This was ASML in November 2020, and the gap kicked off a 5-week run.
questions.lesson_line: Never more than 4% over the buy point. Chasing costs you shares.

wrong.Skip it, any gap over is a chase: A gap isn't a chase by itself. The line is 4% over the trigger.
wrong.Wait for a dip back to 424.70: You might never get it. The buy is at market through the trigger.
wrong.Buy it, but at half size: Nothing says halve it. The stop and the fill set the size.

questions.story: A hold day just closed and the trigger is 424.70. This morning the stock gaps up, and a market buy fills at 429.33.
questions.simple: Buy it. The fill is only 1.1% over the trigger, well inside our 4% limit, so the chase costs very little.

deeper.trap: Don't mix up two numbers. Kell said 3-4% above the averages was too much for him, and that's distance from the averages. Our 4% is measured from the trigger, and the 9 EMA has its own 10% line.

reasons: computed comparison (52.90 against the 50.64 trigger)
rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, never more than 4% above the buy point)
fixed before (the old why mixed Kell's distance from the averages with the trigger)

questions.q: Do you take the new hold day?
choices: No, the weekly cap is used up
Yes, a new hold day is a new try
Yes, at half size to limit risk
No, a losing streak bars buys
questions.answer: No, the weekly cap is used up
questions.why: No. Three tries a week on one stock is the cap, six a month, and you've used this week's three. Here's why it exists. When a stock stops you out again and again, it's telling you something. Most often it's chopping, not trending, and you're forcing it. Step back. If it's still setting up next week, it'll still be there.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week, six a month, on one stock. Then step back.

wrong.Yes, at half size to limit risk: The cap counts tries, not size.
wrong.Yes, a new hold day is a new try: Sure, it's a new try. That's the problem. You're out of tries this week.
wrong.No, a losing streak bars buys: Right call, wrong reason. The cap counts tries on one stock, win or lose.

questions.story: It's Thursday. You've bought this stock three times this week, and each try stopped out. A fresh hold day printed today.
questions.simple: No. You've used this week's three tries on this stock, and when it keeps stopping you out, you step back.

deeper.trap: Don't confuse the try cap with a losing-streak rule. The cap counts tries on one stock, 3 in a week and 6 in a month. The count would be the same if all three had won.

reasons: one cited fact only (h29)
rests on the owner's rulebook (E56, the try cap)

questions.q: Do you trade it?
choices: Pass, it fails both floors
Pass, the pattern isn't clean
Take it, the pattern is clean
Take it, but at half size
questions.answer: Pass, it fails both floors
questions.why: Pass. We trade stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This one's $8 and about $5 million, so it misses both. Thin stocks don't let you get in and out where you want. Your stop at the hold day's low can fill way under it. I wouldn't even keep it on the watchlist.
questions.lesson_line: Liquidity first: $10 or more and $20 million a day. Then look at the chart.

wrong.Pass, the pattern isn't clean: The pattern's fine. The stock is too thin.
wrong.Take it, the pattern is clean: A clean chart on a thin stock is still a thin stock.

questions.story: A neat crossback sets up on an 8 dollar stock that trades about 5 million dollars a day.
questions.simple: Pass. It's under $10 and trades about 5 million dollars a day, too thin to get in and out.

deeper.trap: The floors come before the chart. Even a neat crossback on a thin stock is a pass. We also never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Pass; not a leader by our rule
Pass; its sales growth is missing
Take it; 72 is nearly a leader
Take it at half size for now
questions.answer: Pass; not a leader by our rule
questions.why: Pass. We buy leaders, with an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group. A crossback bets that a strong stock will use its averages as a springboard, as Kell puts it, and a stock rated 72 is not strong enough to count on that. Growth is preferred, but the chart comes first.
questions.lesson_line: We buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in a strong group.

wrong.Take it at half size for now: Size does not fix a leadership gap.
wrong.Pass; its sales growth is missing: Growth is preferred, but the chart comes first. The story's problem is the RS rating.
wrong.Take it; 72 is nearly a leader: Nearly is not enough. The rule is 80 or more.

questions.story: A clean crossback sets up in a stock with an RS rating of 72. The RS rating is the app's score of how strong a stock has been against others.
questions.simple: Pass. We want an RS rating of 80 or more, because a crossback depends on a strong stock springing off its averages.

deeper.trap: 'Close enough' is how rules wear away. Our line is an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group, and 72 is below it. The exception is parabolic and mean-reversion trades, which are other setups.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C31)

questions.q: What's your call?
choices: Pass, Red is mostly cash
Pass, only Green allows buys
Buy a small starter position
Short it, Red favors shorts
questions.answer: Pass, Red is mostly cash
questions.why: Pass. A Red reading means mostly cash for us. In a market like that even good setups fail more, because the market isn't backing them. A great stock doesn't cancel a weak market. Keep it on your radar, though. Leaders that hold up in a Red market are the names to track for when it turns.
questions.lesson_line: Red market, mostly cash. Track the leaders for the turn.

wrong.Buy a small starter position: No starters. We buy once at full size, and Red says mostly cash.
wrong.Pass, only Green allows buys: Yellow and Orange still allow some buys. The reason here is Red.
wrong.Short it, Red favors shorts: Shorts are for weak stocks under the 200-day. This one's a leader.

questions.story: A textbook crossback sets up on a leader. The app's market filter reads Red, the weakest of its four readings.
questions.simple: Pass. Red means mostly cash, so keep the leader on your radar for when the market turns.

deeper.counter: The market reading sets how much risk we take, not whether the chart is good. Green is full risk, Yellow smaller and fewer, Orange A+ only, Red mostly cash. The same setup in a Green market is a different call.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D46, F65)

questions.q: How does that history change your read?
choices: It lowers the grade, a warning
It raises it, a win is due
It only matters in a weak market
It takes the stock off our list
questions.answer: It lowers the grade, a warning
questions.why: It lowers the grade. Three failed crossbacks in a row tell you this stock hasn't respected its averages. So I trust this one less. It's a warning, not a ban. A lower grade means a smaller size, or a pass if I have better ideas. And forget the idea that a win is due. The chart doesn't owe you one.
questions.lesson_line: A stock whose crossbacks keep failing gets a lower grade. Nothing is due.

wrong.It raises it, a win is due: Nothing is due. Past failures are a warning.
wrong.It only matters in a weak market: The stock's own history counts by itself.
wrong.It takes the stock off our list: It lowers the grade. It doesn't ban the stock.

questions.story: A clean crossback sets up in a stock whose last three crossbacks all failed.
questions.simple: It lowers the grade. A stock whose crossbacks keep failing hasn't held its averages, so I trust it less.

deeper.trap: The gambler's trap is thinking a win is due. Past failures say this stock's chart has not held its averages, not that a win is owed. Grade it lower and keep the same stop.

reasons: a proposed card cue

questions.q: Which one would you grade higher?
choices: Crossback A, sooner and stronger
Crossback B, it waited longer
Crossback B, it's already up 15%
Both grade the same
questions.answer: Crossback A, sooner and stronger
questions.why: Crossback A. It's the first rest after a powerful pop, a gap on 3.6x volume, only 5 sessions in. That's a fresh leg with real buyers behind it, and heavy volume on the pop raises the grade. B is late, 18 sessions after a plain pop, and I trust that less. Grading is judgment, so call it a lean, not a score. And either one can fail. The stop decides.
questions.lesson_line: A fresh crossback after a powerful pop grades higher than a late one.

wrong.Crossback B, it waited longer: Waiting longer puts it later in the move. I lean lower on late ones.
wrong.Crossback B, it's already up 15%: Up 15% means further along. That's a reason to trust it less.
wrong.Both grade the same: The pop and the timing both count. A wins.

questions.story: Crossback A comes 5 sessions after a gap-up pop on 3.6x volume. Crossback B comes 18 sessions after a plain 1.0x pop, with the stock up 15% on the quarter.
questions.simple: Crossback A. It comes soon after a strong pop with real buyers, while B is late in its run.

deeper.trap: Lateness and pop strength are grade cues, not gates. A clean-looking crossback can still fail. MU did: it looked clean, simply failed, and the stop did its job. Kell's warning about buying late in an uptrend fits B.

reasons: the pop window is still open (D-076)
'late fails most' is the card's line; our own scan did not confirm it
the A+ and B grade cues are the card's, not measured on our data
flagged for the owner

questions.q: On our card, a rising 200-day is a grade cue, not a gate.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Our card prefers the 200-day rising, meaning higher than it was 20 sessions ago. That is a grade cue, not a gate. The gate is that the hold day closes above the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: A rising 200-day helps the grade. It is not a gate.
questions.simple: Yes, a rising 200-day line is a grade cue on our card, but it is not a gate.

deeper.trap: A rising 200-day is a grade cue, not a gate. The only gate is that the hold day closes above the 200-day. A stock above a falling 200-day can pass the gate, but it earns less credit on the grade.

reasons: one cited fact only (x33)
the rising 200-day is a proposed criterion (xbk.ma200_rising)

questions.q: Take it or pass?
choices: Take it, the hold day is strong
Take it, buy at today's close
Pass, wait for a close over the high
Pass, the gap makes it too risky
questions.answer: Take it, the hold day is strong
questions.why: Take it. Look at the last bar. It came back into the 9 and 20 EMA and closed near its high. That strong close is buyers taking the averages back. The pop was an earnings gap on 3.6x volume, which raises the grade. One thing you'll notice: the 50-day is still pointed down a bit. Price is back over it and the 200-day is rising, so this early in a new leg I'm fine with it. Now set it up right. You buy only when it trades over this bar's high, at market, with the stop under its low. NET did that the next session at 63.34 and ran past 3R the same day.
questions.lesson_line: A hold day that closes strong at the averages gets a trigger over its high.

wrong.Take it, buy at today's close: We don't buy closes. The buy is the trade over the high.
wrong.Pass, wait for a close over the high: No need for a close. You buy as it trades through the high.
wrong.Pass, the gap makes it too risky: A gap on heavy volume is a plus here, not a risk.

questions.simple: Take it. The hold day dipped into the 9 and 20 EMA and closed strong, so buyers took the averages back.

deeper.trap: The trap is hindsight. This one ran past 3R on the trigger day. But in our scan only 28.9% of crossbacks reached 3R before the stop. Judge the hold day before the trigger, not by the result.

reasons: the key is read from a dossier row and a chart, not a rule quote
the chart's bars were not re-checked in this pass

questions.story: This stock gapped up on earnings and popped. It drifted 3 days back into its 9 and 20 EMA. The last bar is the possible hold day.

questions.q: Take it or pass?
choices: Pass, it closed near the low
Pass, the low missed the zone
Take it, the low reached the zone
Take it, buy at today's close
questions.answer: Pass, it closed near the low
questions.why: Pass. The low did its part and reached the zone. Then look at the close. It finished at the bottom of its range, so sellers won the day. Buyers haven't shown up yet. A hold day has to close strong, in the upper half of its range. This was GE on the last day of 2025, closing in the lower 3% of its range. It still triggered and hit 3R. That was luck, not the setup.
questions.lesson_line: A hold day has to close strong. A close near the low is a pass.

wrong.Pass, the low missed the zone: The low did reach it. The close is the problem.
wrong.Take it, the low reached the zone: That's half the job. A weak close means buyers didn't show.
wrong.Take it, buy at today's close: Weak hold day, and we never buy the close anyway.

questions.simple: Pass. It closed near the low, so sellers won the day and buyers haven't stepped in yet.

deeper.trap: The hindsight trap: this near-miss still reached 3R (best 3.5R) before the stop. That was luck. A pass is judged by the setup on the day, not by what came after.

reasons: the key is read from a dossier near-miss row and a chart
the strong-close line is a proposed criterion

questions.story: A stock pulled back to its 9 and 20 EMA after a pop. The last bar is your possible hold day.

questions.q: What do you do with it?
choices: Build your own entry, stop and size
Use their entry, but set your own stop
Copy their stop and size
Buy a starter now, check later
questions.answer: Build your own entry, stop and size
questions.why: Build your own. Pull up the chart and check it yourself: a real hold day, its high for your trigger, its low for your stop. Their stop and size fit their account, not yours. Your size comes from your stop and your risk. Write the entry, stop and size down before the open. Then it's your trade, not theirs.
questions.lesson_line: Never trade someone's post. Make your own entry, stop and size before the open.

wrong.Use their entry, but set your own stop: The entry has to be yours too. Check the hold day yourself.
wrong.Copy their stop and size: Their size fits their account. Yours comes from your own stop.
wrong.Buy a starter now, check later: Check first, plan first, then buy. And no starters.

questions.story: A post says a stock is on its EMA Crossback right now. It gives an entry, a stop and a size.
questions.simple: Build your own plan. Their stop and size fit their account, and your size comes from your own stop.

deeper.trap: A post can name the right pattern and still miss the hold day, the stop or the size. Only your own entry, stop and size make it a plan.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F66 and D39)
fixed before (the old choice said check the base)

questions.q: What is your call?
choices: Take it with a tighter stop
Pass; the 9 slipped under the 20
Take it; the hold day is strong
questions.answer: Pass; the 9 slipped under the 20
questions.why: Pass. With the 9 EMA under the 20, there is no reason to be long, even if the hold day closes strong.
questions.lesson_line: A strong hold day does not repair crossed averages.

wrong.Take it; the hold day is strong: A strong close does not fix the averages.
wrong.Take it with a tighter stop: Pulling the stop in to fit the size is a trap.

questions.story: A leader above its 200-day pops, then pulls back. During the pullback the 9 EMA slips under the 20. The hold day closes strong.

questions.q: What's that telling you?
choices: Be careful, risk appetite is weak
Buy more, they're cheap now
Nothing, each stock stands alone
Good, weak holders got shaken out
questions.answer: Be careful, risk appetite is weak
questions.why: Be careful. When crossback after crossback triggers and fails, buyers aren't following through. Risk appetite is weak. That's feedback from the market, and I listen to it. I grade new crossbacks lower, take fewer, and wait for the ones that work to show up again. One clean setup can still work. But your bar goes up.
questions.lesson_line: When crossbacks keep failing across the market, raise your bar and take fewer.

wrong.Buy more, they're cheap now: Failures aren't a sale. They're a warning.
wrong.Nothing, each stock stands alone: The market's behavior is part of the setup. Ignore it and you keep paying.
wrong.Good, weak holders got shaken out: Failing on low volume is weak demand, not a cleanout.

questions.story: Over two weeks, crossbacks across the market keep triggering and then failing, on low volume.
questions.simple: Be careful. Crossbacks failing all over the market means buyers aren't stepping in, so we grade new ones lower.

deeper.counter: One clean crossback can still work. The cue lowers the grade and doesn't forbid the trade. Check both the stock's own history and how this setup has done across the market lately.

reasons: a proposed card cue built on a market-wide read

questions.q: What do you do about the stop?
choices: Keep the honest stop; cut size or skip
Pull the stop in to fit
Widen the stop
questions.answer: Keep the honest stop; cut size or skip
questions.why: Keep the honest stop. If it does not fit the risk, cut the size or skip. The stop only moves up, never wider.
questions.lesson_line: The stop does not bend to fit the size. The size bends to the stop.

wrong.Widen the stop: The stop only moves up, never wider.
wrong.Pull the stop in to fit: Pulling the stop in to fit the size is a trap.

questions.story: The honest stop is wider than your risk budget allows. A friend says to give it more room.

questions.q: Why do you want a slow drift like this, not a hard drop?
choices: The averages rise to meet price
A hard drop bounces back harder
The 200-day catches it
A drop clears out the sellers
questions.answer: The averages rise to meet price
questions.why: The averages rise up to meet price. When a stock drifts sideways, it isn't giving much back. It's just waiting while the 9 and 20 catch up. That keeps the pullback shallow and your stop close. A hard drop gets to the averages by falling through levels, and that's selling you don't want. This is NOC in November 2014: four sideways sessions onto the 9 EMA, and a 1% stop.
questions.lesson_line: Slow, sideways drift into the averages. Let them come up to you.

wrong.A hard drop bounces back harder: Nothing says that. A hard drop is the violent kind of pullback, and that's a warning.
wrong.A drop clears out the sellers: A hard drop can just keep going. A slow drift lets the averages come up to you.
wrong.The 200-day catches it: A crossback tests the 9 and 20, not the 200-day.

questions.story: A stock popped, then pulled back to its averages in a narrow, sideways range over four sessions.
questions.simple: The averages rise up to meet price, so the pullback stays shallow and your stop stays close.
